nodes.label: Elejalde (1979)
nodes.title: Genetic and diagnostic considerations in three families with abnormalities of facial expression and congenital urinary obstruction: "The Ochoa syndrome".

nodes.label: Elejalde (1979) described 7 patients (4 females and 3 males) from 3 unrelated families, one of them consanguineous (first cousins), with peculiar facies and gestures while smiling and crying. The patients also had hydronephrosis, hydroureter, intravesical stenosis of the ureter, abnormal caliber of the urethra in the prostatic and membranous portions, urethral valves, and an abnormal trabeculated bladder with diverticula and severe mucosal hypertrophy with sclerotic changes.
From genetic analysis of the 3 families, Elejalde (1979) concluded that the condition is probably autosomal dominant, with variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance.
Elejalde (1979) noted that the peculiar facies allows early recognition of the condition, which could help with early assessment and treatment and perhaps lead to a better prognosis.
Elejalde (1979) called the disorder 'the Ochoa syndrome' and suggested that it represents a change in the facial and urinary developmental fields.

Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) described 36 children, seen between 1965 and 1986, who had enuresis and urinary tract infection together with 'inversion' of facial expression when laughing. Urologic work-up found mild neuropathic bladder in all patients, and most had severe urinary tract damage. About two-thirds of the patients also had moderate to severe constipation.
Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) proposed the name 'urofacial syndrome' for this disorder.

Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) stated that the clear association between distorted facial expression and neuropathic bladder, which leads to genitourinary tract damage, should prompt urologic evaluation of individuals with 'inversion' of facial expression.

Ochoa and Gorlin (1987) concluded that the disorder is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner. They based this on its occurrence in multiple sibs, normal parents, increased parental consanguinity, and an equal sex ratio.

Wang et al. (1997) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive disease characterized by congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression; patients present with enuresis, urinary tract infection, hydronephrosis, and voiding dysfunction resulting from neurogenic bladder.

Wang et al. (1997) performed a genome screen combining homozygosity mapping and DNA pooling in 20 selected UFS patients, one patient pool, and 3 control pools of unaffected relatives; of 36 random markers, D10S677 showed linkage and association with UFS, with a significant excess of homozygosity in patients compared with unaffected relatives (P < 10(-6)) and allele frequency differences between patient and control pools.

Wang et al. (1997) fine-mapped the UFS gene with 10 additional markers spanning 22 cM using haplotype (linkage disequilibrium) analysis: all 31 patients were homozygous for D10S1726 and D10S198, about 5 cM telomeric to D10S677, versus only 12% of unaffected relatives (P < 10(-19)). Recombinations in patients heterozygous at flanking markers D10S1433 and D10S603 placed the gene within a 1-cM interval on chromosome 10q23-q24.

Wang et al. (1999) used homozygosity mapping in American patients of Irish heritage to show that urofacial syndrome in these patients mapped to the same 10q23-q24 region previously identified in families from Colombia. They concluded that the syndrome is genetically homogeneous.

Wang et al. (1999) built a physical map of the UFS critical region on 10q23-q24 and identified new polymorphic markers in it. Haplotype analysis with these markers placed the UFS gene within a single YAC clone of 1,410 kb.

Wang et al. (1999) found the exact location of the GOT1 gene, which encodes glutamate oxaloacetate transaminase, within the new UFS critical region and determined its genomic structure. Mutation analysis excluded GOT1 as the UFS gene.
Wang et al. (1999) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive disorder marked by an abnormal facial expression and urinary abnormalities.

Chauve et al. (2000) reported the first European cases of urofacial syndrome, in a French family. Haplotype analysis in this family, compared with previously reported haplotypes in Colombian and American patients, was compatible with localization of the critical region to chromosome 10q23-q24.
Chauve et al. (2000) concluded that the haplotype results in a French family favored the hypothesis of genetic homogeneity of urofacial syndrome.

Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) reported 3 European patients with urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome, a disorder originally described in Colombian patients. They suggested that the syndrome may be missed because the urinary problems vary and the characteristic facial grimacing is not recognized.
Garcia-Minaur et al. (2001) stressed that an early diagnosis of urofacial syndrome has important consequences for managing the urinary problems and for their prognosis.

Wang et al. (2003) built a genomic sequence map covering the urofacial syndrome interval on chromosome 10q23-q24, which had earlier been placed in a region of about 360 kb by homozygosity mapping. They narrowed the critical region to 220 kb. This region contains the newly identified ACDP1 gene and part of the GOT1 gene, which had already been excluded as a UFS candidate.

Wang et al. (2003) searched ACDP1 extensively in UFS patients, including the coding region, the 5-prime and 3-prime untranslated regions, the promoter, and the exon/intron junctions. They found no pathogenic mutation.
From their analyses, Wang et al. (2003) concluded that the same chromosome 10q gene causes UFS in all patients, across multiple ethnic groups.
Wang et al. (2003) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare disorder with congenital obstructive uropathy and abnormal facial expression, caused by a single recessive gene.

Derbent et al. (2009) reported a patient from Turkey with urofacial syndrome. The authors described it as the first published case of the syndrome in that country. The patient had been followed for recurrent urinary tract infection and vesicoureteral reflux and was not diagnosed until age 16 years. The authors stressed that recognizing the characteristic facial grimacing allows early diagnosis, which matters for managing the urinary problems.

Derbent et al. (2009) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive disorder. Patients have an 'inverted' facial expression, so that they appear to be crying when they smile. They also have serious urinary tract problems, including enuresis, urinary tract infection and hydronephrosis. Some severely affected patients become hypertensive and progress to end-stage renal disease.

Aydogdu et al. (2010) reported 11 patients with urofacial syndrome from 5 families from Turkey, followed for a median of 32 months (range, 2 to 44 months). The authors described the syndrome as having uropathy and facial abnormalities, and stressed that early diagnosis is crucial for managing urinary problems caused by a dysfunctional bladder.
Aydogdu et al. (2010) described urofacial (Ochoa) syndrome as a rare autosomal recessive condition that occurs in both sexes.

Pang et al. (2010) identified loss-of-function mutations in the HPSE2 gene in all patients with urofacial syndrome they studied, who came from Colombia, the United States, and France. HPSE2 lies in the chromosome 10q24 region that the authors had previously found by homozygosity mapping.
Pang et al. (2010) suggested that because UFS patients completely lack HPSE2 function, HPSE2 may be important for the coordinated action of the muscles used in facial expression and urine voiding.
Pang et al. (2010) noted that they had previously mapped the urofacial syndrome gene to chromosome 10q24 by homozygosity mapping.

Daly et al. (2010) described urofacial syndrome (UFS) as a rare autosomal recessive disease characterized by facial grimacing when attempting to smile and failure of the urinary bladder to void completely despite a lack of anatomical bladder outflow obstruction or overt neurological damage. They noted that UFS individuals often have reflux of infected urine from the bladder to the upper renal tract, with a risk of kidney damage and renal failure.
By whole-genome SNP mapping in one affected individual, Daly et al. (2010) defined an autozygous region of 16 Mb on chromosome 10q23-q24.
Within the 10q23-q24 autozygous region, Daly et al. (2010) identified a 10-kb deletion encompassing exons 8 and 9 of the HPSE2 gene in an individual with urofacial syndrome.

nodes.label: Daly et al. (2010) identified homozygous exonic deletions, nonsense mutations, and frameshift mutations in the HPSE2 gene in 5 further unrelated families with urofacial syndrome, confirming HPSE2 as the causative gene.
Daly et al. (2010) did not identify HPSE2 mutations in 4 additional patients with urofacial syndrome, which they concluded indicated genetic heterogeneity.

Daly et al. (2010) showed that HPSE2 is expressed in the fetal and adult central nervous system, where they suggested it might be involved in controlling facial expression and urinary voiding. It is also expressed in bladder smooth muscle, which they considered consistent with a role in renal tract morphology and function.
